summary: This document reserves ranges of numbers for experimenting in specific protocols, namely IPv4, IPv6, ICMPv4, ICMPv6, UDP and TCP headers, where the need was identified. It also describes numbers already reserved for this by other documents, so experiments need not use real assigned values.

eli5.summary: Scientists testing a new gadget need a safe number that nobody else uses. This sets aside some numbers just for tests so they don't collide with real ones.

questions: which ip protocol numbers are for experiments
subtitle: Reserved numbers in IP, ICMP, UDP and TCP headers that experimenters can use without colliding with real assignments.

tldr.problem: Anyone testing a new protocol feature needs some protocol number or constant to put in a header, even in a closed lab, and picking a random real one risks clashing with existing uses.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC reserves experimental values in IPv4, IPv6, ICMPv4, IPv6 Neighbor Discovery, UDP and TCP headers, and lists the ones other documents already set aside, mostly following the two-value RFC 3692 style (253 and 254).
tldr.outcome: Experimenters get known values that firewalls and other tools can recognize as experimental, but the values must only be used in explicitly configured experiments and never shipped as defaults.

today: RFC 4727 is a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It serves as the record of the experimental values it reserves.

sections.title: Why Reserve Experimental Values
sections.content:
When experimenting with or extending protocols, it is often necessary to use some protocol number or constant to test the new function, even in a closed environment. RFC 3692 recommends assigning option numbers for experiments and testing. This document records several such assignments for the number spaces whose IANA rules are described in RFC 2780, and it follows the form of that document.

The RFC warns that it is not appropriate to simply pick one of these values and hard code it into a system. Sections 1 and 1.1 of RFC 3692 should be read first.
sections.eli5: These are practice numbers. You can borrow them for a test, but you should not build them permanently into a real machine.

sections.title: IPv4 Header Fields
sections.content:
The Version field is always 4. For Type of Service, RFC 2474 already defines Pool 2 (all code points xxxx11) as Experimental/Local Use, so nothing new is needed, and the ECN field has no free code points.

For the Protocol field, RFC 3692 allocates two experimental code points, 253 and 254.

No experimental IPv4 unicast addresses are defined. For some experiments the private ranges of RFC 1918 may help, but other special-purpose IPv4 addresses are not appropriate. For multicast, the globally routable group 224.0.1.20 is set aside, and this document assigns the link-local group 224.0.0.254 and the scope-relative group 254.

One IPv4 option number, 30, is assigned with every combination of the copy and class fields, giving four option type codes.
sections.eli5: The IPv4 header gets a couple of test protocol numbers, one test multicast group and one test option, so a lab can try out new ideas.

sections.title: IPv6 Header Fields
sections.content:
The Version field is always 6. As in IPv4, the Traffic Class needs nothing new because of the Pool 2 code points, and RFC 3692 allocates 253 and 254 for the Next Header field.

There are no RFC 3692-style experimental IPv6 unicast addresses yet. Unique Local Addresses may be useful for some experiments, but the documentation prefix must not be used. The multicast group FF0X::114 is set aside for experimentation at all scope levels, and smaller scopes are handy because they do not leak out of the boundary of the experiment.

A single Hop-by-Hop and Destination option type is assigned, with all possible values of the act and chg fields, giving eight option type codes. The IPv6 Routing Header gets two routing types, 253 and 254.
sections.eli5: IPv6 gets the same kind of test numbers, plus a test multicast group that works at every distance.

sections.title: ICMP and Neighbor Discovery
sections.content:
This document assigns two ICMPv4 type numbers, 253 and 254. ICMP code values are allocated per type, so experimental codes cannot be assigned here.

For ICMPv6, RFC 4443 already includes experimental types for Informational (200, 201) and Error (100, 101) messages. In IPv6 Neighbor Discovery, the Type field is the ICMPv6 Type, the Code field is unused, and two Neighbor Discovery Option Types, 253 and 254, are assigned.
sections.eli5: Error and status messages also get a few test labels, so new kinds of messages can be tried without confusing real ones.

sections.title: UDP and TCP
sections.content:
Two system ports, 1021 and 1022, are reserved for experimentation for both UDP and TCP.

In the TCP header there are not enough reserved bits to allocate any for experiments. Two TCP option kinds, 253 and 254, are reserved for experimenting with TCP options.
sections.eli5: Two test doors, numbered 1021 and 1022, are kept free for experiments, and two test labels are kept for new TCP extras.

sections.title: The IANA Assignments
sections.content:
Section 8 summarizes the new registrations. Each is marked RFC3692-style Experiment and carries a footnote: these values are only appropriate in explicitly configured experiments, and they MUST NOT be shipped as defaults in implementations.

The registries touched are the IPv4 multicast addresses, IPv4 option numbers, IPv6 option types, IPv6 Neighbor Discovery option formats, IPv6 routing types, ICMPv4 type numbers, system port numbers and TCP option numbers.
sections.eli5: Each test number is written in the official list with a note: use it only for tests you set up yourself.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Production networks do not necessarily support experimental code points, and unsupported ones can disrupt a network. The reach of an experiment should be evaluated before it crosses extended domains such as the public Internet.

Firewalls and intrusion detection systems often rely on unambiguous readings of these fields. A known experimental value lets them take a known action. The experimental IPv4 options are not covered by IPsec AH calculations, so their use cannot be authenticated. For the IPv6 options, the chg value decides whether the option is included.

Within one administrative domain, each code point should be used consistently. Across domains, experimenters should assume that other experiments may use the same code points at the same time and interfere.
sections.eli5: Test numbers can confuse the real network, and two people may pick the same one, so tests should stay small and be handled with care.
